notation.meaning: Power for predictor $j$ and its estimate
Constructed variable for the score test
Intercept, slope and error in the transformed regression

blocks.md: Box-Cox asks which power of the outcome makes a regression behave. Box-Tidwell asks the same question about the explanations instead: which power of income, or of education, makes its relationship with the outcome a straight line? It estimates one power per predictor. A power of one means leave the predictor alone, a power near zero means take its log, and a power near two means square it. Alongside each estimate comes a test of whether the predictor needs transforming at all.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It turns the visual hint of a bent component-plus-residual plot into an estimated transformation with a p-value.

where $T(x, \lambda)$ is the Box-Cox power transformation ($x^{\lambda}$, read as $\ln x$ at $\lambda = 0$) and the predictors must be positive. The $\lambda_j$ are estimated by maximum likelihood. The test of $H_0: \lambda_j = 1$ ("no transformation") is the $t$ test on the **constructed variable** $x_j \ln x_j$ added to the untransformed regression: a significant coefficient means $x_j$ wants a power other than 1.

sections.heading: Worked example: prestige on income and education

blocks.md: Controlling for a quadratic in the percentage of women (102 occupations):

Income's power is essentially zero, so use $\log(income)$, matching what the [Component-Plus-Residual Plot](note:component-plus-residual-plot) suggested; education's is about 2, so add a square. Both tests reject $\lambda = 1$ at 5%.

blocks.md: The constructed-variable plots are added-variable plots for $x\ln x$: a clear slope (strong for income, milder for education) means the predictor wants a transformation.

- **Applying it to predictors with zeros or negatives.** The powers need $x > 0$ (the percentage of women has zeros, which is why it enters as a polynomial instead).
- **Using the exact estimate.** Round to an interpretable power (log, square root, square), as with Box-Cox.
